subject: Civil Engineering
title: Sulfate Attack
description: Learn Sulfate Attack in one minute.

hook.text: Foundations in sulfate-rich soil expand and crumble — the concrete destroys itself from within.

buildup.text: Sulfates react with aluminate compounds in cement, forming ettringite — a crystal that expands.

discovery.text: Type V cement has low aluminate content — it resists sulfate attack in harsh soils.

twist.text: Low w/c ratio also helps — denser concrete slows sulfate penetration dramatically.

climax.text: The Middle East uses sulfate-resistant concrete extensively — gypsum-rich desert soils demand it.

punchline.text: Know your soil chemistry. The wrong cement in the wrong ground self-destructs.

quiz.question: How does sulfate attack damage concrete?
options: Sulfates dissolve the aggregate, leaving hollow voids
Sulfates react with cement compounds to form expanding crystals that crack the concrete
Sulfate gases corrode the rebar inside the concrete

details.summary: Sulfate attack occurs when dissolved sulfates in soil or groundwater react with compounds in hardened cement paste to form expansive products like ettringite and gypsum. This expansion causes cracking, softening, and eventual disintegration of concrete exposed to sulfate-rich environments.
details.whyItMatters: Sulfate attack can destroy foundations, underground structures, and pipelines in sulfate-bearing soils within a decade. Using sulfate-resistant cement in these environments is essential for durability.
takeaways: Sulfates react with cement compounds to form expansive ettringite and gypsum
Expansion of reaction products cracks concrete from the inside out
Type V portland cement has low tricalcium aluminate for sulfate resistance

faq.question: Where are sulfate-rich environments commonly found?
faq.answer: Sulfate-rich soils are common in arid and semi-arid regions where evaporation concentrates sulfate minerals. Industrial wastewater, agricultural runoff, and some groundwater sources also contain sulfates.

faq.question: How can concrete be designed to resist sulfate attack?
faq.answer: Use sulfate-resistant cement with low tricalcium aluminate content. Replace cement with pozzolans like fly ash or slag that consume calcium hydroxide. Reduce permeability with low water-cement ratios. Provide protective coatings or membranes between concrete and sulfate-bearing soil.
